decisionGap: Readers see BRRRR as a loop that recycles the same cash. They cannot tell from competitor explainers what stops it: the refinance must wait for lender seasoning, the new loan is sized on the appraised value, and inside six months the delayed-financing limit ties the loan to the purchase investment (on our reading of the wording, not the rehab spending; ask the lender). A worked break-even shows how high the appraisal must land.
method: Modeled: a deterministic scenario (evidence/brrrr-method/run.py) with illustrative inputs ($150,000 purchase, $3,000 purchase closing costs, $40,000 rehab) and illustrative assumptions (75% loan-to-value, 2% refinance cost) at three appraised values; the rules are reported from the Fannie Mae Selling Guide (B2-1.3-03) and IRS Publication 527 fetched 2026-11-04.

provenance.scopeAndLimits: Hypothetical scenario with author-chosen inputs; the 75% loan-to-value and 2% refinance cost rate are assumptions, not lender limits and not Fannie Mae figures (the Eligibility Matrix was not retrievable). Fannie Mae rules apply to loans sold to Fannie Mae; other lenders set their own rules. Rent, cash flow, taxes and the new interest rate are not modeled. No claim that we completed a BRRRR purchase.

findings.claim: Fannie Mae cash-out refinance: existing first mortgage being paid off must be at least 12 months old; at least one borrower on title six months before disbursement; listed properties must be off the market
findings.label: reported

findings.claim: Delayed financing exception for purchases within six months: arms-length purchase, no mortgage used, no liens, funds documented, and new loan no more than the documented initial purchase investment plus financed closing costs, prepaid fees and points, subject to max LTV on current appraised value
findings.label: reported

findings.claim: Residential rental property is depreciated over 27.5 years under GDS; land is not part of the depreciation basis; a rehabbed house is placed in service when ready and available for rent
findings.label: reported

findings.claim: Illustration: $193,000 total cash invested; at a $230,000 appraisal, assumed 75% LTV and 2% cost, $23,950 stays in the deal; at $200,000, $46,000; at $260,000, $1,900
findings.label: modeled

findings.claim: Illustration: full cash-out at the assumed 75% LTV and 2% cost needs an appraisal of about $262,585 (1.36 times the cash invested)
findings.label: modeled

findings.claim: Illustration, on our reading of the rule (Fannie Mae does not address repair spending; the author counts purchase price plus purchase closing costs as the $153,000 initial investment): inside six months a loan capped at that amount plus the 2% financed costs (about $156,122) leaves $40,000 in the deal at $230,000 and $260,000 appraisals
findings.label: modeled

finding: BRRRR recycles cash only when the appraised value after repairs times the lender's loan-to-value limit, less refinance costs, covers what the investor put in. In our modeled example (assumed 75% loan-to-value, 2% costs) a $230,000 appraisal leaves $23,950 of $193,000 in the deal and full recovery needs about $262,585. Under Fannie Mae's delayed-financing exception, a refinance inside six months is capped by the documented purchase investment; on our reading of that wording (Fannie Mae does not address repair spending, so ask the lender) it does not include the later repair spending.
conditions: Modeled scenario with author-chosen inputs; the loan-to-value and cost assumptions are not lender limits; rules cited are Fannie Mae's, and other lenders differ; rent, cash flow, the new rate, taxes and holding costs are not modeled; investor-property loan-to-value limits are in the Fannie Mae Eligibility Matrix, not read.
whatWouldChange: A lender's actual maximum loan-to-value for an investment-property cash-out refinance, a different appraised value, a change to the Fannie Mae seasoning or delayed-financing rules, or the investor's cash flow after the refinance.
counterexample: At a $200,000 appraisal the same project leaves $46,000 in the deal (run.py low scenario); on our reading of the delayed-financing wording, inside six months the cap leaves $40,000 even at a $260,000 appraisal because the loan is capped near $156,122.
limitations: Illustrative inputs and assumptions; one scenario; no cash flow, taxes, new interest rate or holding costs; delayed-financing cap modeled, on the author's reading, as purchase price plus purchase closing costs plus the 2% financed costs; Fannie Mae does not state how repair spending is treated.
unknowns: Any lender's actual investment-property LTV and rate
Non-Fannie-Mae lender seasoning rules (DSCR and portfolio lenders)
Appraisal outcome for any specific property
selectedMedium: text with one scenario table (three appraised values, two refinance paths) and a break-even sentence; no interactive calculator in this run (scenario is deterministic and reproducible from the saved script; a calculator would need a verified LTV table)
takeaway: BRRRR can recycle most or all of an investor's cash only when the appraisal after repairs is high enough that the loan covers the money in the deal: in our modeled example that took about $262,585 on $193,000 invested. It fits an investor who can wait out lender seasoning and is buying below the finished value; it does not fit anyone counting on a low appraisal, on a refinance inside six months to recover repair spending (on our reading of the wording; ask the lender), or on a payment the rent cannot cover. Evidence basis: Fannie Mae Selling Guide and IRS Publication 527 (reported) plus our scenario (modeled). Changes with the lender's real loan-to-value limit and the appraisal. Next step: ask a lender for its seasoning rule and maximum investment-property loan-to-value before buying.
